sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles the backbone of the central Apennines between the reliefs SE of the Rieti plain (to the north-west) and the higher Sangro R. valley (to the south-east), across the Fucino plain. This Source falls within the core of the SW-dipping, inner Abruzzo normal fault system, marking the western extensional border of the central Apennines.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show a particularly dense intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) to damaging seismicity within the area. Furthermore, this source has been hit by some complex, destructive earthquakes; the main ones are the 9 September 1349 (Mw 6.5, Aquilano), and 13 January 1915 (Mw 7.0, Avezzano). The latter is certainly one of the most studied earthquakes of the Italian seismic history, also given its occurrence within the XXth century. Finally, the 7 May 1984 (Mw 5.9) Appennino abruzzese earthquake has occurred in the southern end of this source.
A segment of this Source was responsible for the catastrophic 1915 event that has fostered a remarkable amount of research. To the south of the Source, a further fault caused the 1984 event, which proves to be quite significative due to its position at the passage between the SW-dipping (in Abruzzo) and NE-dipping (in Molise) large normal fault systems from the central to the southern Apennines.
Some segments of this Source have been associated with key destructive earthquakes that have occurred in this area. For an in-depth analysis of seismogenesis in this region, the reader can refer to the Individual Sources in this Database.
The strike of the Source was based on that of the mapped structures. The dip was based on geological and seismological data. The rake represents pure extension, based on geological observations. The minimum and maximum depth were based on geological data. The slip rate was in part based on geological and paleoseismological data.

pictures.t: Structural map of the Fucino basin and surroundings
pictures.c: Seismotectonic map showing the trace of the Ovindoli-Pezza fault system, major active faults of the area and distribution of recent seismicity. The surface breaks of the 1915 earthquake are highlighted by dots (from Piccardi et al. [1999]).

pictures.t: Regional evolution of the Liri, Fucino and L'Aquila basins
pictures.c: Deformation evolution of the Abruzzi region. According to this model, beginning with Early Pleistocene times, the bending of the compressive margin caused left-lateral strike-slip kinematics along N160- to NS-striking faults (from Galadini [1999]).
Geological and geomorphological map of the Fucino Plain and location of surface ruptures produced by the 1915 earthquake (from Michetti et al. [1996]).

pictures.t: Summary map of the epicentral area of the 7 May 1984 earthquake
pictures.c: Epicentral region of the 7 May 1984 earthquake and surroundings, showing trend of major normal faults and area of densest aftershock activity (from Westaway et al. [1989]).
Historical and instrumental earthquakes (a), and geological sketch (b) of the central Apennines (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).
Location and parameters of the main earthquakes of the central Apennines and the associated Composite Sources (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Views on rate of activity of the faults
pictures.c: Diverse views on the rate of activity of faults of the central Apennines. Notice that individual faults are often interpreted differently by different research groups (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the central Apennines
pictures.c: Synoptic view of the active faults and the seismogenic sources (DISS, version 3.1.1) of the central Apennines. Notice that the main extensional sources terminate to the northwest and to the southeast at the transverse OASL and ORL, respectively (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini Line, seismogenic sources, and geofluids
pictures.c: Relationships between tectonics and geofluids in the inner Apennines. An alignment of thermal springs and CO2 emissions highlights the presence of the Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini Line (OASL), a major tectonic lineament, that plays a role in controlling the segmentation of seismogenic faults in central Italy (Vannoli et al., [2021]).

pictures.t: EMS-98 Intensity map of the 7 May 1984 earthquake
pictures.c: Revised intensity map of the 7 May 1984 earthquake, in terms of new macroseismic data and European Macroseismic Scale (EMS-98). The 7 May shock provoked widespread moderate damage, worsened in some cases by the aftershock of 11 May (Graziani et al., [2017])

pictures.t: Surface traces of active or potentially active faults in central Italy
pictures.c: A number of surface active or potentially active faults identified and mapped by Bosi (1975) in a large region stretching from the Apennines piedmont east of Rome to the Adriatic coast  (Vannoli et al., [2012])

pictures.t: Surface normal faults and their slip directions in central Italy
pictures.c: Surface active normal faults offsetting the base Holocene and striking parallel to the thrust belt of the central Apennines, with their fault-slip directions (panel b), and the Quaternary basins in the hanging walls (panel c; Roberts and Michetti, [2004])

pictures.t: Quaternary faults and topographic profiles across the Abruzzi Apennines
pictures.c: Main Quaternary faults (panel A) and topographic profiles across the Abruzzi Apennines with location of the main Quaternary faults (panels B and C; Galadini and Messina, [2004])
